newsitem.title: USA: Intervention jitters linger in wake of G7--experts.
newsitem.headline: Intervention jitters linger in wake of G7--experts.

text.p: Nearly two weeks after a meeting of Group of Seven (G7) financial leaders, concern about intervention remains focused primarily on the Bank of Japan (BOJ) as other G7 nations can likely tolerate a moderately stronger dollar, U.S. experts said.
Since the G7 issued a statement on February 8, the dollar has hit a 34-month high of 1.7050 marks and a 37-month peak of 1.4907 Swiss francs, but it has failed to reach 125 yen.
"I agree that everybody's nervous about possible intervention from BOJ," said Norihiko Ogihara, a vice president at Mitsui Trust and Banking.
"That's why most players feel much more pressure on dollar/yen rather than dollar/mark and dollar/Swiss," Ogihara said.
Experts noted a lingering fear in the market that the BOJ may intervene if the dollar breaks above the 125 yen barrier.

John Rothfield, an international economist at Nationsbanc, said speculators are more willing to take on European central banks than the BOJ, mainly because it is felt administrations in Japan and the U.S. possibly have a vested interest in stopping dollar/yen rising because of the growing trade imbalance between the two countries over the past four months.
Japan's trade surplus with the U.S. jumped 81.6 percent in January from a year earlier.

The dollar has appreciated about 56 percent against the yen since it registered a post-World War II low of 79.75 yen on April 19, 1995. Versus the mark, the dollar has risen some 26 percent since tumbling to a post-World War II low of 1.3438 marks on March 8, 1995.
Both the BOJ and the Bundesbank have employed jawboning to stem the dollar's rise, but German central bank officials have sent mixed signals this week.
Buba President Hans Tietmeyer repeated in interviews that he is against any further rise in the dollar against the mark.
Yet Buba council member Ernst Welteke reportedly said a dollar level between 1.70 and 1.75 marks posed no major danger of imported inflation to Germany.
"They are not saying the same story," said Ogihara, who concluded the Bundesbank is only concerned about the pace of the dollar's rise.
The U.S. is not Germany's primary trading partner. Perhaps that is one reason why Germany may be able to stomach a higher dollar/mark exchange rate.

Very little of Germany's foreign trade is conducted with the U.S., said Rothfield. "There's not that direct relationship between a change in dollar/mark and a change in German trade or import prices," he said.
Most of Germany's foreign trade is with the Netherlands, Belgium, France, Italy and others, where exchange rates have been quite stable, Rothfield said.
A statement released after the latest G7 meeting said the major misalignments in exchange markets noted in the April 1995 communique have been corrected.
The 1995 communique was backed up by well-timed joint central bank intervention, which played a key role in helping the dollar recover.
On Friday morning, the dollar traded near 122.50 yen and 1.6830 marks.

Last June, then-Deputy U.S. Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers outlined ideal conditions for successful intervention. Summers told a conference that intervention is most effective in cases where "it was a surprise and a signal of policy intervention."
The statement provided some experts with clues as to why the Treasury might not intervene on its own behalf near term.
"The element of surprise is not there yet," said Michael Faust, global portfolio manager at Bailard, Biehl and Kaiser.
"The market is actually, if anything, maybe more wary than it should be (about intervention)," Faust added.
He also noted that neither the U.S., Germany nor Japan is prepared to back up intervention with monetary policy action.
Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin has repeatedly said U.S. dollar policy remains unchanged and that a strong dollar is in the U.S. interest.
Faust said intervention would indicate the Treasury wants a weaker dollar and he doubted the Treasury wanted to send that message.
In short, Faust concluded the U.S. would not be the instigator of any near-term intervention.

In discussing why the Federal Reserve would not intervene near-term on the Treasury's behalf, Nationsbanc's Rothfield noted that the broad trade-weighted value of the dollar is only marginally higher in the past year.

"From the U.S. perspective, the dollar isn't a major concern right now," he said. "So therefore, I wouldn't rule out Fed intervention, but it would really be on behalf of the other central banks. It wouldn't be on (Treasury's) account."
